items.title: Cost cutting is not cost reduction; builders and trades face a test
items.description: A reliable estimate of the tariff burden on a typical newly built American home puts the cost at $12,919, or about $4.88 per square foot. That is before accounting for broader inflation in construction labor, transportation, services and other inputs that homebuilders must absorb while trying to make their homes affordable to increasingly price-sensitive customers. This informed baseline calculation of tariff impact at the new-home level, developed by homebuilding supply-chain consultancy Strategem through its Strategy Pulse Pro platform, updates the National Association of Home Builders ' April 2025 builder-reported tariff-cost estimate of $10,900 to reflect subsequent trade-policy changes. The model distributes tariff exposure across 17 material categories, with hardware and fasteners, steel products, lumber, cabinets, windows and aluminum accounting for some of the highest estimated costs. By its nature, Strategem’s tally is a modeled cost burden, not a direct measure of tariffs paid on every home or of the amount passed through to buyers. Still, it illustrates a difficult dilemma for homebuilders, and one none of them can simply avoid: Costs imposed upstream cannot necessarily be recovered downstream. And in that downstream market, households increasingly lack the financial capacity or confidence to buy homes at the prices builders need to charge. That predicament, predictable in a falling market, is a reflexive homebuilding firm response that reverberates through homebuilding’s wider ecosystem like a bad-trip flashback. Homebuilders are looking to their suppliers, manufacturers, distributors, and trade contractors to shoulder more of the financial pain. It's a law of dismal science physics during a downturn: Wringing a bit of margin improvement by most builders means squeezing suppliers' margins into further negative territory. The danger is that some builders may, and often do, push their business partners beyond what they can reasonably absorb. This tactic, seductive as it may seem as a way to claw back input cost reductions, mostly serves as a temporary fix. Ultimately, such quick fixes undermine the very production capacity, service reliability, and competitive supplier pools they will need to survive the downturn and recover. The shock absorbers are wearing thin Homebuilders have spent much of the past two years using price reductions, mortgage-rate buydowns and other incentives to preserve sales velocity. Those concessions have helped sustain production, but they have also eroded the earnings cushion – the “shock absorber” – that previously allowed many builders to absorb rising costs without substantially disrupting operations. The squeeze is occurring on both sides of builders' income statements. According to NAHB's November 13 analysis of Producer Price Index data, goods used in new residential construction rose 9.8% year over year in October, while service inputs increased 11.3%. The combined input index rose 10.4%, including a 5.8% increase in building-material prices. These are input-price indexes, not equivalent percentage increases in the total cost of constructing a house. Still, they reveal why slowing demand has not delivered the broad-based cost relief builders might otherwise expect. The pressure is particularly difficult for smaller builders and suppliers with limited financial reserves. They must keep enough business flowing to cover fixed costs while protecting the margins and working capital required to remain viable. When cost savings aren't really savings Ken Pinto, a longtime homebuilding strategic-sourcing executive and co-founder of Strategem, and a friend of The Builder's Daily , believes the industry risks conflating two fundamentally different types of cost reduction. Purchasing departments are reporting savings from increasingly competitive bidding, he says, but those reductions often come from suppliers sacrificing profitability rather than from lasting improvements in how homes are built. "When you reduce costs by going out to bid, going out to bid, going out to bid, you're not taking cost out of the supply chain; you're taking margins out," Pinto says. This self-preservatory instinct among homebuilding business decision-makers has important, potentially risky, consequences. A trade contractor who accepts a lower price to keep crews working may provide immediate relief to a builder's direct costs, but the underlying costs of labor, transportation, insurance, equipment, and materials may remain unchanged. When demand eventually recovers, those concessions may disappear. More troubling, some suppliers may not survive long enough to participate in the recovery. Pinto points to manufacturers facing higher costs for steel, copper and resin-based products while struggling to secure corresponding price increases. Their customers may be able to delay accepting price increases, but the underlying costs do not disappear simply because builders refuse to pay them. The resulting margin compression can become unsustainable. A fragile supply chain beneath the surface Conversations with homebuilding purchasing professionals suggest that the opportunities for further reductions vary considerably by category. Some material suppliers remain willing to compete aggressively for market share, particularly in areas where slower construction activity has created excess capacity. But trade contractors face different circumstances. Years of declining production volume have already weakened some local subcontractor businesses. In some markets, established trade firms have closed, while others struggle with cash flow, payment disputes and mechanics' liens. At the same time, immigration enforcement has reduced labor availability in trades including framing, concrete, masonry, roofing, electrical work and painting. items.title: Beyond commission splits: How wellness benefits give brokerages a recruiting edge
items.description: By many estimations, real estate professionals are facing the most challenging housing market in recent memory in 2027 . Unlike in the past, many will be doing so with access to more resources than ever designed to ensure they are feeling healthy, at the peak of their game and ready to tackle whatever the 2027 housing market throws at them. This is because over the past year, several brokerages announced a variety of wellness programs and health insurance opportunities they are now offering to agents, who as independent contractors, typically do not have access to things like insurance through their brokerage. Since the start of 2026, ENRG Realty , Compass International Holdings , Equity Union Real Estate and John R. Wood Properties have announced the launch of health insurance or wellness benefits initiatives. “We were founded on Maslow Hierarchy of Needs, so health insurance fits right in with some of the core basic values that we need to provide to our agents so they can be successful and thrive,” Erinn Nobel, the co-founder and president of ENRG Realty and a HousingWire Woman of Influence award winner, said. “In order for our agents to function at a high level, they can’t be sitting at home worried about an illness or being able to pay their bills because they don’t have health coverage. It is a foundational offering and a benefit for us to be able to provide it for our agents.” Nobel said that while some Realtor boards or associations offer health insurance, there is often just one policy option, something she experienced first hand after moving to Alaska from Washington state. “It was great to be able to access insurance through our board, but there was only one plan, so you couldn’t shop around,” Nobel said. “It just didn’t sit well with me that my options were so limited.” A similar experience with challenges accessing insurance for his family is also what inspired Harma Hartouni , the CEO of Equity Union Real Estate, a RealTrends Verified brokerage, to begin providing his agents with access to group-style health coverage options, including a nationwide PPO network, through a partnership with Trident BPO . When he approached the executive team about launching this initiative, Hartouni said they were a bit divided as to whether or not they should do this. “Some thought the agents wouldn’t care, but some of our managers thought it was great,” Hartouni said. “Ultimately, our agents are our clients, and I knew that if these people were not healthy or not in a clear mindset in this challenging market, they would not function well.” In the current uncertain economic environment, Hartouni added that the offering has also provided many agents, who previously had access to insurance through a spouse who lost their job, a level of peace of mind that they couldn’t previously provide. “The consistent feedback from agents is that they are saving money and are able to see better doctors,” Hartouni said. Agent recruitment ‘magnet’ Nobel said she’s heard similar feedback from her agents. After rolling out the program, Nobel said she and her team received countless messages from agents saying thank you. Beyond better serving existing agents, Nobel said the program also helped ENRG Realty with agent recruitment. “It has become an attraction magnet for us. Savvy agents that have been in the industry for a while are starting to really compare brokerages and look at what benefits they get from each brokerage and the different values they provide,” Nobel said. “If an agent already has access to health insurance through a spouse or partner, then this may not convey the same value as it would to a self-employed single mom who would love to have access to health care.” Hartouni has also noticed the agent recruitment benefits of offering health insurance. “The smart broker is looking for producing agents that are in the middle of their career, where they still have plenty of years left in the business to learn and grow, but have already begun to establish themselves,” he said. “But these agents often have families to think about and how can we help them have one less thing to worry about? We can provide them with access to health insurance.” Helping agents find paths to better health While John R. Wood Properties is not providing agents with access to health insurance, the brokerage recently announced it was providing its agents with access to individualized coaching focused on their personal well-being and professional development, through a partnership with HatchPath . Through the program, agents can gain access to coaching support across a wide range of areas including nutrition, stress management, mental resilience, leadership, career development and major life transitions. “People are just so burn[ed] out in general and everybody is on edge from personal challenges, financial challenges, family challenges. I just thought what better way to support our people than to give them access to coaching,” Corey McCloskey, the president of John R. Wood Properties, a RealTrends Verified brokerage, said. “I think a lot of us who run businesses have realized that you bring your whole self to work. You can’t just turn off what's happening in your personal life when you walk into your office — it affects you whether you realize it or not.” While still in the early stages of the rollout, McCloskey said she has seen her agents and staff use HatchPath coaching for help with everything from financial planning to fitness and overall physical wellness. items.title: FHA’s reverse mortgage book faces headwinds from home prices, fewer payoffs
items.description: The Federal Housing Administration ’s fiscal year 2026 actuarial report to Congress says the Home Equity Conversion Mortgage ( HECM ) reverse mortgage portfolio remains a small but volatile slice of the FHA's Mutual Mortgage Insurance Fund, showing that its stand-alone capital ratio dropped significantly in the wake of lower endorsement numbers over the past year. The report , released Nov. 16, found that the MMI Fund's overall capital ratio dropped slightly during the year ending Sept. 30, moving from 11.47% last year to 10.29% this year. The current figure, however, is roughly five times higher than fund's statutory minimum requirement of 2%. Looking exclusively at the HECM portfolio, the capital ratio was down significantly from 24.06% in FY 2025 to 5.43% in FY 2026. The FHA attributed this decline mainly to macroeconomic dynamics and program-specific cash flows. HECM remains profitable but capital buffer tightens The reverse mortgage portfolio, which accounts for less than 4% of the fund's insurance in force, is “much more sensitive to home prices,” the report explained. Slower home price appreciation and updated macroeconomic forecasts have increased projected losses for the HECM program. In addition, loan payoffs — which represent more favorable recovery outcomes than other disposition methods like foreclosures — have become less common and have pushed losses higher. The agency also noted that the HECM program “spent substantial capital resources on assignment claims in FY 2026, reducing available cash.” These claims, which are generated when FHA acquires loans that hit the 98% maximum claim amount threshold, are a known driver of volatility in the HECM book. They remain a key cost to monitor for reverse mortgage issuers and servicers . While the federally insured reverse mortgage portfolio is still in the black, the takeaway from the report is that its capital support can change rapidly due to shifts in home price appreciation, payoff behaviors and the frequency of assignment claims. These factors drive FHA policy decisions, as well as Ginnie Mae execution in the HECM Mortgage-Backed Securities ( HMBS ) market. HECM volume falls again, proprietary loans fill the gap The report illustrates that FHA-insured options remain central to the wider reverse mortgage market, even as volumes edge lower. In FY 2026, FHA insured 24,162 HECMs representing a maximum claim amount (MCA) of $12.81 billion. Endorsements were down about 14% from the 28,149 HECMs endorsed in FY 2025. MCA volume also fell from about $15.5 billion in 2025 to roughly $13.5 billion in 2026. But even with that pullback, the HECM program “remains a large part of the market,” according to the report. Historic data reinforces the sector’s structural shift. HECM endorsements peaked above 110,000 in 2009 with roughly $30.5 billion in MCA. Volumes have trended lower for more than a decade, with visible rebounds in 2020–2022 during a period of low interest rates and high home price growth. But higher rates and slower price growth since 2023 have softened demand. To fill the gap, lenders are focusing on proprietary reverse mortgages through their retail, wholesale and correspondent channels. The wider availability of these products has propelled a shift in market share as private-label loans accounted for more than 60% of reverse mortgage volume in September, according to New View Advisors . "I think that product diversity is great because we're able to serve more clients that the FHA product wouldn't handle," Jesse Allen , president of 55+ lending at Rate , told HousingWire 's Reverse Mortgage Daily (RMD) at this month's National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association (NRMLA) Annual Meeting & Expo. He said these may be " mass affluent clients who have home values of $2 million or $3 million, and they really want to tap their equity without the debt service to achieve their goals," but they can also be clients who don't fit the HECM qualification requirements and are using reverse mortgage proceeds to consolidate debt. "This is another regulatory guideline NRMLA has advocated for. 'Hey, we're paying off consumer debts. Let's not count that toward the the qualification process.' Proprietary allows us to do that and HECM does not," Allen said. Portfolio characteristics, sensitivity to home prices FHA's FY 2026 report includes a dedicated HECM chapter that details borrower profiles and loan features. These include HECM loan purposes (such as home purchases versus refinancing of existing debt), payment plan options, interest rate types, borrower ages and maximum claim amounts and initial draws by recent borrower cohorts. The agency emphasizes that its actuaries model HECM cash flows separately from forward mortgages and explicitly stress-test the reverse portfolio under varying home price appreciation scenarios. Home price appreciation assumptions affect multiple levers across the program — including the available equity at the end of the loan, the size of recoveries through property sales and the loss severity tied to claims. Indirectly, home price growth can also impact payoff incentives. The report notes that waning price growth in 2026 had an “outsized negative impact” on HECM capital compared with forward mortgages. This underscores why even modest regional or national home price corrections are more consequential for HMBS investors and issuers than for traditional mortgage-backed securities . The stand-alone capital ratio of 5.43% for the HECM portfolio suggests that FHA still has room to absorb stress, but far less cushion than in the prior three years when the ratio ranged between roughly 16% and 25%. It also may create more difficulty for industry advocates in their push to reduce upfront mortgage insurance premiums. items.title: REPORT: Bears In Talks For Public Financing For Arlington Heights Stadium
items.description: The ongoing Chicago Bears stadium saga has taken another turn, with the team reportedly negotiating with a suburb of its hometown for taxpayer-backed funding. The team, state lawmakers and the government of Arlington Heights are discussing a plan that would use local tax revenue generated by a proposed $3.5B stadium and nearby properties to back tax-exempt construction bonds, Crain’s Chicago Business reports . Parking and amusement taxes are among the potential sources targeted for revenue, although the amount is unknown. Bisnow/Ryan Wangman “What we’re doing here is somewhat complicated, and the Bears will be primarily paying for the stadium, but the stadium authority would be floating the bonds,” state Sen. Bill Cunningham told Crain’s. The negotiations come as Illinois lawmakers consider House Bill 0958 , which would allow qualifying Cook County municipalities to create public stadium authorities capable of owning facilities, issuing bonds and leasing stadiums to professional sports franchises. While the legislation passed the Illinois Senate in May, it ultimately stalled in the House. A revised proposal of the bill would expand the state’s sales tax and revenue bond program to include stadium properties, allowing for sales tax revenue to support bonds financing infrastructure improvements. The revised proposal was not discussed during the first week of the Legislature’s veto session, and it is not guaranteed to make it through the House and Senate in the last three days, scheduled Dec. 1-3. However, Gov. JB Pritzker has made it a priority, Crain’s reported. The public ownership proposal marks a shift from the team’s earlier pursuit of a team-owned stadium funded by payments in lieu of taxes . The proposed arrangement would exempt the stadium from property taxes , a significant consideration for the proposed redevelopment of the 326-acre Arlington Heights property that the Bears purchased in 2023 for $197M . An analysis released by the Cook County Treasurer’s Office in May estimated that the team could save more than $39M annually under the earlier megaproject tax proposal. But that estimate doesn’t directly apply to the current stadium authority arrangement under discussion. While H.B. 0958 sits on desks in Illinois, the team already announced in June that it plans to move to Hammond, Indiana. items.title: REIT Sells 400-Unit Arlandria Apartment Community For $69M
items.description: UDR has offloaded a suburban D.C. asset that it had owned for a quarter of a century. The REIT sold Presidential Greens, a 1930s-era garden-style community in what is called Arlandria — a Northern Virginia neighborhood on the border of Arlington and Alexandria — after holding on to it since 2002. Google Maps The Presidential Gardens multifamily community at 3904 Executive Ave. in Alexandria, Virginia A joint venture between Blackfin Real Estate Investors and JSB Capital Group purchased the 396-unit property at 3904 Executive Ave. for $69M, the buyers and Berkadia announced Monday. UDR revealed in its third-quarter earnings report earlier this month that the property was under contract for the disclosed price. UDR didn’t respond to Bisnow ’s request for comment. The REIT, which owns 9,129 units in greater D.C., according to its Q3 supplemental , originally paid $30M for Presidential Greens. The buyers said in a press release that the asset benefits from D.C.-area multifamily deliveries “slowing considerably,” the need for attainable housing for workers like teachers and public servants, and the property's proximity to employment nodes. The purchase represents Blackfin and JSB’s 13th transaction together, Blackfin co-founder and Managing Partner Doug Root said, adding that it had been a few years since the last one. “We have been focused on trying to find a well-located, strong cash flowing asset for our next investment,” he said in the release. “Recent market conditions have made that more challenging but the location and profile of Presidential Greens fit our objective to a tee.” Berkadia represented the seller and secured financing for the buyer. Senior Managing Director Brian Crivella led the investment sales team, and Managing Director Brian Gould and Senior Managing Director Patrick McGlohn led the mortgage banking team. Truist provided acquisition financing, the terms of which weren’t disclosed. “Presidential Greens represents a compelling investment opportunity in one of Northern Virginia's most established rental markets,” Crivella said in a separate release from the brokerage. “With nearly 400 apartments in a highly accessible Alexandria location, the property offers scale, a strong occupancy history and enduring housing demand — attributes that continue to attract capital.” Northern Virginia accounted for 70% of the $4.2B in multifamily investment sales that occurred across the D.C. metro during the first three quarters of the year, according to Northmarq . This year's multifamily sales volume has already surpassed the figure for the entirety of 2025. items.description: London-based finance firm Mount Street Group has hired a team of seasoned primary and special servicing professionals to establish a Dallas hub. The expansion deal will add almost $1.4B of assets to its approximately $30B U.S. servicing book, according to an announcement on Monday . The group, led by former Credit Suisse credit chief Paul Smyth, will oversee the firm’s U.S. securitized products, collateralized loan obligation and special servicing business. Wikimedia Commons/Mx. Granger Mount Street Group's London headquarters at 100 Wood St. “The securitized products and special servicing markets require experience, judgment and a disciplined approach to execution,” Smyth, who was named managing director and head of securitized products in the U.S., said in a statement. “Mount Street’s platform gives us the ability to bring those capabilities to clients at greater scale, supported by a strong global infrastructure and a clear commitment to growth in the U.S. market." The team is made up of executives from Broadsword Investors, co-founded by Smyth, and Goldersun Loan Servicing, both Dallas-based firms. The servicing book was acquired from Goldersun, according to a Mount Street spokesperson. Throughout his 40-year career, Smyth has managed more than $55B in loan resolutions. He served as Credit Suisse ’s global chief credit officer and president of Greystone ’s special servicing portfolio before starting his own specialty finance firm. Broadsword was founded alongside Cary Williams, who will also join Mount Street, focusing on new client initiatives and asset management. Mount Street’s new team also includes Joe Beggins, who was CEO of General Electric Capital Loan Services and GEMSA Loan Services, the subsequent commercial mortgage servicing joint venture between GE and CBRE . Beggins has held leadership positions at other CRE firms since, including managing member of Goldersun. He will oversee asset management and process enhancements for investors at Mount Street. Goldersun CEO Terry Clay will move to Mount Street, where he will serve as head of the surveillance and reporting team. He previously worked at Hudson Advisors. John Roach, who worked with Smyth at other companies, including Greystone, will lead the Dallas team's primary servicing and CLO operations components. In a statement, Rawle Howard, head of Mount Street USA, said the addition of the new team “marks a meaningful acceleration of Mount Street’s U.S. growth strategy.” “Their market credibility, technical expertise and deep experience across securitized products, B-Piece investing, CMBS, special servicing and asset management are highly complementary to our existing platform and will immediately enhance the depth of service we can provide to clients,” Howard said. “This transaction is not just about adding scale; it is about adding the right people, capabilities and leadership to support the next phase of our U.S. growth.” Founded in 2013, Mount Street has more than €163B of assets under administration and €31.9B in assets under valuation, or roughly $177.5B and $34.7B, respectively. It employs more than 200 people across Europe and the U.S. The global third-party loan servicing and credit management business established its North American branch in 2017. Mount Street USA is headquartered in Atlanta. items.title: Stuck: How a frozen housing market is hitting buyers, sellers and the economy
items.description: 'The scary part' It all has Ryan Deighan, who wants to buy a home, wondering if he ever will. "I genuinely don't know, and that's the scary part," he said. Deighan and his wife have been renting in Boston for six years. He is a chiropractor; she works in private equity. Even with a combined salary of more than $200,000 a year, he says they're stuck. Boston chiropractor Ryan Deighan is unsure if he'll ever be able to buy a home. CNBC "Making what I am and what my wife makes, it just feels like we're on paper doing well, but it feels like we are still kind of fighting to put down certain amounts toward a house," Deighan said. Being priced out of homeownership, he said, is changing what he called his "checklist" of how he once pictured his future. "You graduate college, you find someone, you get married, you have the home with the white picket fence and the dog, and then the kids," he said. "That just looks a little different for us." Sellers are stuck, too The numbers don't just affect would-be buyers. They are hitting sellers, too. Robin Welch has been living in her Cleveland-area home for more than 20 years. Her children are now grown and moved out. She would like to downsize to a condominium, but the math doesn't make sense — in part, because her current interest rate is much lower than any new rate she could get. This has been dubbed the mortgage "lock-in effect." "It actually costs more money to buy less of a home," said Welch. "I would have to pay into an HOA, which would be another monthly expense on top of increased property taxes and increased interest rate." Welch has also done upgrades to her home over the years and doesn't want to have to start doing that on another home. Get Property Play directly to your inbox CNBC's Property Play with Diana Olick covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, delivered weekly to your inbox. Subscribe here to get access today . Welch is part of why the housing turnover rate, which is how often homes get new owners, has now dropped to just 3.8% a year, well below the 5% rate in the decade following the financial crisis, according to Cotality. In addition, the national mobility rate, which is how often people move from region to region, has been falling for two years. It now sits at 8.3%, down from 11.1% a decade ago, according to Harvard's Joint Center for Housing Studies tabulations of U.S. Census Bureau data. Mobility hit a high of nearly 18% in the late 1980s. "It's largely because of the interest lock-in effect, but also because of home prices just being so high," said Riordan Frost, senior research analyst at Harvard's JCHS. "Those things combined have made it hard both for existing homeowners to move and for people to get into homeownership." Americans have nearly $35 trillion of their wealth locked up in housing, a record high , according to Cotality. But the slowdown in the housing market, Frost said, impacts the accumulation, handover and use of that wealth. It also affects the labor market. "Any kind of potential job would have to really outweigh … the price of taking that mortgage with a higher rate, or the price of moving, or the price of getting into a higher rent unit," Frost said. The wealth gap between homeowners and renters now is nothing short of massive. The most recent survey of consumer finances last year by the Federal Reserve showed that the median homeowner net wealth is about 43 times the median renter net wealth. "It has kind of knock-on effects for the rest of the economy. It has effects on the labor market and how good of a match we can get between employees and employers. It has an effect on education. It has an effect on just GDP growth," said Zhao. Buyers back out When homes aren't selling and people aren't moving, those who work in that business are stuck as well. The entire housing ecosystem is churning much more slowly, and the sudden jump in mortgage rates is causing deals to fall apart. "Right after Labor Day, we went live with a bunch of listings. They all went under contract over the asking price," said Dana Bull, a real estate agent in the Boston suburbs. But then rates spiked. "It was a shock to the system," Bull said. "I think all of them came back on the market. We fell out of contract." Asked if she is seeing colleagues leaving the market, she answered: "People are thinking about it. It's tough." Dana Bull, a real estate agent in the Boston suburbs. CNBC The economy has lost close to 2,000 jobs in real estate and leasing over the past year and 4,400 jobs in residential construction, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. Jobs in the mortgage industry have been falling since June and are down 38% since their last peak in the second quarter of 2021, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association. That was when mortgage rates were less than half what they are today. Shant Banosian, president of Rate and the top mortgage originator in the U.S. by dollar volume, said his business is down about 30% this past year. "Whenever change happens quickly, there's a slowdown," said Banosian, who has been in the business for 23 years. "It requires more of us to go out and advise, educate and guide. So, what I experienced was I just needed to spend more time on marketing, branding, relationship building. The conversations are longer because people want more information to try to navigate this market." Bull agrees. She said her job has gotten harder as well. "We've done double the work this year, having homes go under contract, fall out of contract, putting them back under agreement, but definitely more negotiating," she said. "That's sort of my plea to both buyers and sellers: We need to get back to a space where we're comfortable negotiating." items.title: Buying a Home Soon? This Overlooked Open Enrollment Perk Could Save You Thousands in Legal Fees
items.description: Buying a home comes with enough expenses already. Between inspections , title insurance , closing costs, and a stack of paperwork that seems to grow every day, it's easy to lose track of what you're paying for. But what if your employer could help cover some of the legal bills? It's a possibility many homebuyers may overlook during open enrollment, when employees are typically comparing health insurance premiums and retirement benefits rather than thinking about hiring a lawyer. Employer-sponsored legal plans, offered through companies such as LegalShield , MetLife and ARAG , can provide access to attorneys for a modest monthly fee. A real estate attorney can review a purchase agreement, make sure inspection and financing contingencies actually protect the buyer, check the deed and title, examine mortgage documents, and represent a buyer at closing. Depending on the plan, some or all of that may be covered. Jago Gavin , a LegalShield representative who works with employer groups, tells Realtor.com® that the real value is having someone to consult before signing something you might not fully understand. "The law is not logical; it's legal," Gavin says. That's relevant when buying a house , where an unfamiliar contract provision can have expensive consequences. Gavin recalls a LegalShield member whose attorney spotted a potentially unfavorable mediation clause in real estate paperwork and recommended changing it before the buyer signed. The potential savings can run from hundreds to thousands of dollars. But there's a catch: Not all legal plans offer the same services, and buyers need to know what they're getting before signing up. Legal help for about $20 a month? Group legal plans work much like other voluntary workplace benefits. Employees pay a monthly premium, usually through payroll deductions, in exchange for access to specified legal services. The price can be surprisingly affordable. In a review of publicly available employee benefits documents, Realtor.com found a plan offered to employees of financial technology company Fiserv through MetLife for $15.50 monthly. LegalShield's published employer plans generally cost about $19 to $25 a month, depending on the coverage and employer. That's roughly $186 to $300 annually, potentially less than the cost of a single consultation with a private attorney. The plans typically provide access to participating law firms that handle matters ranging from contract reviews and consumer disputes to estate planning. Some cover specific services in full, while others offer discounted rates for legal work outside the plan. Loading... A real estate attorney can review a purchase agreement, make sure inspection and financing contingencies actually protect the buyer, check the deed and title, examine mortgage documents, and represent a buyer at closing. Universal Images Group via Getty Images How much could a homebuyer actually save? ContractsCounsel , an online marketplace connecting clients with attorneys, reports that lawyers on its platform charged an average flat fee of $620 to review a real estate purchase agreement, based on completed projects. Compare that with LegalShield's published Choice plan, which costs $21.95 monthly, or $263.40 over a year. If an employee uses the plan for comparable document-review work without additional charges, the potential savings could be about $350. But reviewing a contract and representing someone throughout a real estate transaction are two very different services. LegalShield's published employer-plan documents include certain residential mortgage-document reviews but specifically exclude an attorney's attendance at closing. Documents must also be provided at least five business days before the scheduled closing. Other plans offer broader coverage. An ARAG legal plan available to University of California employees, for example, pays participating attorneys for covered services that include reviewing and preparing home purchase documents and attending a closing. California doesn't generally require attorneys at residential closings, but the benefit illustrates how coverage can extend beyond reviewing paperwork. The MetLife plan offered to Fiserv employees also lists home purchases and sales among its covered services. MetLife plan descriptions published by several other employers go further, listing deeds, boundary and title disputes, and property tax assessments—handy if a new owner wants to challenge a tax bill after the purchase. Employees should still check precisely what their particular plan includes. And even comprehensive coverage won't eliminate ordinary closing expenses. Buyers are generally still responsible for title insurance, recording fees, taxes and other third-party charges. Is there a downside to using a plan attorney? New York real estate attorney Adam Leitman Bailey sees the obvious appeal: lower costs. But he questions whether attorneys with busy, established practices have much incentive to participate in programs requiring them to accept reduced fees. For a relatively straightforward transaction, that might not matter much, he says. But complicated purchases can be another story. "When something goes wrong, and this is the biggest investment of your lifetime, you'd better believe that you should be hiring the best attorney you can," Bailey tells Realtor.com. That doesn't mean attorneys participating in group plans are necessarily less qualified. It does mean buyers should ask about their experience, particularly if a transaction involves title disputes, unusual contract provisions, or other complications. Availability matters, too. Gavin acknowledges that LegalShield sometimes encounters coverage gaps in rural areas, where the nearest participating firm may be hours away. items.title: Why an Uninsulated Garage Can Wreak Havoc on Your Home This Winter
items.description: An uninsulated garage might seem like no big deal, but come the winter months, it can do more harm than good. In fact, when a garage lacks proper insulation during the colder months, frozen pipes, heat loss, and damaged items are bound to arise. Fortunately, insulation solutions and preventive measures can help you avoid these issues while protecting your garage, your car, and your home . Risks of uninsulated garages during the winter An uninsulated garage in the winter months can cause a chain reaction of issues to the home itself. One of the most common risks is frozen pipes. “When the plumbing or water lines located in the garage get exposed to below-freezing temps, they may freeze and cause water damage,” explains Chris Boyle , in-house repair tech at Parts Town Home and Fix.com in Nova Scotia . Additionally, improperly insulated garages can prompt heat loss throughout the entire home. “Many poorly insulated garages share foundations with homes. As a result, cold air may circulate through the living spaces and force families to turn up their heating systems,” says Boyle. Not only does this put a strain on HVAC systems, it can also drive up monthly heating bills. Plus, poor insulation may damage items stored in the garage, particularly car batteries, which can lose charge or fail completely. Loading... Winterizing your garage can save you more money than you might imagine. Getty Images How to tell if your garage is insulated So, how do you know for sure whether your garage is insulated? On a cold day, compare the temperature inside your garage to the outside. If your garage feels as cold as the outdoors, or if the rooms adjacent to it are always noticeably colder in the winter, there’s a good chance it’s not insulated. “You can also inspect the walls and ceiling for visible insulation. On the garage door, thin or hollow panels usually indicate a lack of insulation, while thicker panels often mean insulating material is present,” explains Paul Sharpe , owner at Surfside Garage Doors in Toms River, NJ . Practical insulation solutions and preventive measures to explore Once you determine you have an uninsulated garage, here are several tips to keep on your radar. Insulate your garage For a faster, practical insulation solution, seal any of the bottom gaps under your garage door with rubber weatherstripping. “If your budget and resources allow, however, the most effective way to retain heat in your garage is to insulate all the walls with fiberglass insulation,” says Chris Hunter , director of customer relations at ServiceTitan in Glendale, CA . Regardless of your choice, these solutions will help decrease your energy bill and create a more comfortable environment. Upgrade to an insulated garage door Since the garage door is the largest opening in your home, investing in an insulated garage door may be worthwhile. Entry-level insulated doors typically provide an R-value between 6 and 9, while higher-end models can reach R-values of around 20. “The higher the R-value, the higher the insulation capabilities and less heat loss that will occur,” explains Sharpe. Store your items properly You don’t have to expose your valuables to the risks of an uninsulated garage. “To avoid damaging your items in the garage during winter, you may either elevate them or bring them inside your insulated home,” says Tamer Sayed , licensed HVAC technician and the owner-operator of Tamas Mechanical in Mississauga, Ontario . Consult an HVAC professional Before the winter begins (or even after, if you missed the boat), consult an HVAC professional for an insulation evaluation. The pro can determine whether your garage is properly safeguarded for the season and recommend the best next steps.

items.title: Number of High-Intent Home Shoppers Dropped to a New Low Last Quarter as Stubborn Mortgage Rates Stymied Demand
items.description: Number of High-Intent Home Shoppers Dropped to a New Low Last Quarter as Stubborn Mortgage Rates Stymied Demand Buffalo, Hartford, Providence and San Francisco remain the most competitive markets Written by Treh Manhertz on November 23, 2026 The number of engaged home shoppers — Zillow users who save or share a for-sale listing — fell 4.8% from a year earlier to 3.5 per listing in the third quarter of 2026, the lowest level since Zillow began tracking the metric in 2023. Engaged shoppers per listing declined from last year in 44 of the 50 largest metro areas, led by Seattle, Washington, D.C. and Louisville. Four of the six major markets where engagement increased were in Florida. Luxury homes are drawing more than twice as many engaged shoppers per listing as starter homes. Home-buying demand last quarter hit the lowest level Zillow has tracked. Mortgage rates rose from July through September, leaving fewer serious shoppers in the market. The long-running inventory recovery is also spreading that dwindling demand across more homes. The number of engaged home shoppers per listing fell to 3.5 nationally in the third quarter of 2026. An engaged shopper is defined as a Zillow user who saved or shared a for-sale listing, signaling real interest beyond casual browsing. Agent activity is excluded from this analysis. The 3.5 engaged shoppers per listing last quarter is down 4.8% from a year earlier and the lowest level for any quarter since Zillow began tracking the metric in the second half of 2023. The pullback was widespread, with engagement down from last year in 44 of the 50 largest metro areas, although major Florida markets were an exception. Higher mortgage costs are the most likely driver of the drop in demand. Mortgage rates averaged 6.43% in Freddie Mac’s July 2 Primary Mortgage Market Survey , and rose to 7.28% by October 1. That jump in rates is enough to increase the monthly mortgage payment on a $400,000 home by nearly $200, from $2,008 to $2,189 (assuming a 20% down payment). Typical mortgage costs rose year over year in August, September and October, ending a 10-month streak of annual declines. Inventory keeps growing as shoppers pull back, helping bring down the number of engaged shoppers per listing. As of October, for-sale inventory has risen on an annual basis for 35 consecutive months, though it remains 14.4% below pre-pandemic norms. New listings have been a mixed bag, up on a year-over-year basis in just six of the past 12 months, suggesting the inventory buildup is more a result of homes staying on the market longer than a surge of new sellers. Nearly every major metro saw home shoppers pull back The pullback was widespread. Seattle saw the steepest drop in engaged shoppers per listing, down 17.1% from a year earlier. Washington, D.C. (-15.5%), Louisville (-14.3%), Salt Lake City (-13.7%) and Minneapolis (-13.4%) followed. Only six large metros posted gains, and four of them are in Florida: Jacksonville (+12.2%), Miami (+8.7%), Tampa (+4.2%) and Orlando (+0.8%). San Francisco (+5.1%) and Birmingham (+0.9%) were the others. Buffalo (6.7 engaged shoppers per listing), Hartford (6.2), Providence (6.1), San Francisco (6) and San Diego (5.2) had the most engagement last quarter. Despite its 8.7% year-over-year bounceback, Miami was one of the coolest markets with just 1.9 engaged shoppers per listing. Only Houston (1.6) had fewer. Luxury engagement holds steady while starter-home interest slides Luxury listings — homes among the top 5% most valuable in a given metro — typically drew 6.4 engaged shoppers last quarter, flat from a year earlier. Starter homes — homes in the 5th to 35th percentile of home values in a given metro — typically drew 2.9 engaged shoppers, down 8.2% year over year. This reflects the “K-shaped” housing market that has emerged. Economic headwinds such as slower hiring and rising inflation are prompting many households to delay major financial commitments like a home purchase. Higher-income households are in a different position. Stock market gains have boosted buying power, while higher mortgage rates have little impact on those who can make an all-cash purchase. Rental market is seeing spillover demand With for-sale demand waning, many would-be buyers appear to be turning to rentals instead. Nationally, rental demand is up 22.1% from a year earlier, according to Zillow’s October Rental Market Report . Demand for single-family rentals is up 24.3%, roughly double the 12.1% rise for apartments. The typical single-family rent is $2,243 a month, about $360 less than the monthly cost of owning a single-family home with 20% down. items.title: 2027 Global Investor Outlook
items.description: 2027 Global Investor Outlook Nov 23, 2026 | 10 min read Global real estate opportunities are evolving as capital becomes more targeted and selective. Download report View interactive report Experts David Amsterdam President, Capital Markets | U.S. Rachael Rothman Director, National Capital Markets Research Steig Seaward Senior Director, National Research Share Article More selective approach unlocks new opportunities Global real estate enters 2027 with investors more accustomed to a higher cost of capital and increasingly ready to deploy. As valuations recalibrate and buyer and seller expectations converge, the conditions for greater transaction activity are beginning to emerge. However, the path to returns is changing. With less scope to rely on yield compression, investors are placing greater emphasis on income growth, asset quality and active value creation. The 2027 Global Investor Outlook combines insights from Colliers' capital markets experts around the world with findings from the 2027 Global Investor Survey to explore where opportunities are emerging and what will shape capital deployment in the year ahead. Five catalysts for a stronger global investment market in 2027 As investors adapt to a higher cost of capital, the outlook points to a more selective market, with greater emphasis on income growth, asset quality and active value creation. Greater pricing equilibrium as buyer and seller expectations converge. Rental growth , supported by constrained development and resilient occupier demand. items.title: Mapping a $702 billion risk
items.description: In California, the question of utility infrastructure maintenance arrived on the floor of the state legislature this year. The debate centers around the contentious question of how much financial responsibility should utility companies face if their equipment causes a catastrophic wildfire. But there is another, equally pressing, question: Where exactly does infrastructure pose wildfire risk to homes, and how big could the bill be if a wildfire sweeps through the area? Cotality analyzed this question across the service territories of California’s three major investor-owned utilities: Pacific Gas & Electric (PG&E), Southern California Edison (SCE), and San Diego Gas & Electric (SDG&E). It turns out that over one million residential properties are at moderate or greater risk of wildfires. That number of homes translates to $702 billion in total reconstruction cost value. Utility service territory risk profiles Utility service territory Properties at moderate+ wildfire risk Estimated reconstruction cost value (RCV) Pacific Gas & Electric (PG&E) 458,286 ~$277 billion Southern California Edison (SCE) 431,470 ~$301 billion San Diego Gas & Electric (SDG&E) 171,790 ~$124 billion Combined total 1,061,546 ~$702 billion Data source: Cotality, 2026 ‍ That number isn’t the full story. California is served by 85 electric utility providers . A good number of those utilities serve densely populated, wildfire-prone areas. In the state’s legislative seat of Sacramento County, PG&E only serves 2,500 homes. And those homes are on flat, irrigated land, which brings down the utility’s total home exposure risk. The wildfire risk in that area falls primarily on Sacramento Municipal Utility District utilities. Navigating that boundary division for a cohesive mitigation strategy requires coordination. Coordination requires insight. ‍ Dive deeper Understand the nuance of wildfire risk Well-priced policy The cost of wildfires is high. In California, they strain insurance operations. They can leave utilities struggling to maintain solvency. Even in some of the wealthiest ZIP codes in the U.S., their destruction is leading to homeowners putting off mortgage payments in the wake of their destruction. ‍ ‍ These acute events ignite without warning, but they don’t have to arrive without preparation. The California bill calls on utilities to have a wildfire mitigation plan. But to plan, you need to understand the risk. Risk is quietly shifting the narrative of home ownership. Buyers, lenders, and insurers need property-level clarity before the total price can be judged with confidence, and they can implement risk mitigation to build long-term resilience. Knowing the size and scope of the risk exposure will aid lawmakers and communities with objective hazard assessment, community hardening, and mitigation.
